{{Short description|Algorithm in numerical analysis}}
'''Miller's recurrence algorithm''' is a procedure for the backward calculation of a rapidly decreasing solution of a [[three-term recurrence relation]] developed by [[J. C. P. Miller]].<ref name=Miller/> It was originally developed to compute tables of the modified [[Bessel function]]<ref name=Olver/> but also applies to Bessel functions of the first kind and has other applications such as computation of the coefficients of [[Chebyshev polynomials#As a basis set| Chebyshev expansions]] of other [[special functions]].<ref name=Nemeth/>

Many families of special functions satisfy a recurrence relation that relates the values of the functions of different orders with common argument <math>x</math>.

The modified Bessel functions of the first kind <math>I_n(x)</math> satisfy the recurrence relation
:<math>I_{n-1}(x)=\frac{2n}{x}I_n(x)+I_{n+1}(x)</math>.
However, the modified Bessel functions of the second kind <math>K_n(x)</math> also satisfy the same recurrence relation
:<math>K_{n-1}(x)=\frac{2n}{x}K_n(x)+K_{n+1}(x)</math>.

The first solution decreases rapidly with <math>n</math>.  The second solution increases rapidly with <math>n</math>.  Miller's algorithm provides a numerically stable procedure to obtain the decreasing solution.

To compute the terms of a recurrence <math>a_0</math> through <math>a_N</math> according to Miller's algorithm, one first chooses a value <math>M</math> much larger than <math>N</math> and computes a trial solution taking initial condition <math>a_M</math> to an arbitrary non-zero value (such as 1) and taking <math>a_{M+1}</math> and later terms to be zero.  Then the recurrence relation is used to successively compute trial values for <math>a_{M-1}</math>, <math>a_{M-2}</math> down to <math>a_0</math>. Noting that a second sequence obtained from the trial sequence by multiplication by a constant normalizing factor will still satisfy the same recurrence relation, one can then apply a separate normalizing relationship to determine the normalizing factor that yields the actual solution.

In the example of the modified Bessel functions, a suitable normalizing relation is a summation involving the even terms of the recurrence: 
:<math>I_0(x)+2\sum_{m=1}^\infty (-1)^mI_{2m}(x)=1</math>
where the infinite summation becomes finite due to the approximation that <math>a_{M+1}</math> and later terms are zero.

Finally, it is confirmed that the [[approximation error]] of the procedure is acceptable by repeating the procedure with a second choice of <math>M</math> larger than the initial choice and confirming that the second set of results for <math>a_0</math> through <math>a_N</math> agree within the first set within the desired tolerance. Note that to obtain this agreement, the value of <math>M</math> must be large enough such that the term <math>a_M</math> is small compared to the desired tolerance.

In contrast to Miller's algorithm, attempts to apply the recurrence relation in the forward direction starting from known values of <math>I_0(x)</math> and <math>I_1(x)</math> obtained by other methods will fail as rounding errors introduce components of the rapidly increasing solution.<ref name=Hart/>

Olver<ref name=Olver/> and Gautschi<ref name=Gautschi/> analyses the error propagation of the algorithm in detail.

For Bessel functions of the first kind, the equivalent recurrence relation and normalizing relationship are:<ref name=Arkfen/>
:<math>J_{n-1}(x)=\frac{2n}{x}J_{n}(x)-J_{n+1}(x)</math>
:<math>J_0(x)+2\sum_{m=1}^\infty J_{2m}(x)=1</math>.

The algorithm is particularly efficient in applications that require the values of the Bessel functions for all orders <math>0 \cdots N</math> for each value of <math>x</math> compared to direct independent computations of <math>N+1</math> separate functions.
